claims.text: Replacing the EAM reference potential with an MTP trained on TaVCrW ab initio data and replacing TI with FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP+FEP method will reproduce the TOR-TILD free energy to within 0.5 meV/atom.
Achieving the stated accuracy requires the MTP to capture the relevant solid and liquid phase-space distributions, including SRO effects.
Electronic excitations may affect solid and liquid TaVCrW.
SRO stabilizes the solid phase by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
The relevant validation temperature range is 2000-2400 K.
The supercell must be sufficiently large to capture SRO correlations.
High-temperature magnetic fluctuations are neglected in the proposed calculations.
GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding or overbinding errors for V and Cr may affect the calculations.
An MTP can serve as a computationally efficient surrogate for the DFT forces otherwise required during thermodynamic integration.
FEP can estimate free-energy differences directly from MTP-generated phase-space samples.
Using FEP bypasses the slow, stepwise thermodynamic-integration path.
The accuracy of FEP depends on the MTP-generated statistical distribution matching the ab initio distribution.
The calculated melting temperature and thermodynamic properties will match the TOR-TILD baseline within an error margin expressed as 0.5 meV/atom.
A supercell containing more than 100 atoms is typically sufficient to resolve the characteristic SRO correlation length.
Restricting validation to 2000-2400 K ensures that the liquid is stable and that SRO is not washed out by thermal disorder.
Errors associated with V and Cr functional behavior may propagate through the MTP training data.
Neglected high-temperature magnetic fluctuations could cause free-energy errors exceeding 0.5 meV/atom.
A TaCr benchmark with available high-precision TOR-TILD results can be used to compare MTP+FEP against TOR-TILD.
The hypothesis is falsified if the free-energy discrepancy exceeds 0.5 meV/atom or the cost reduction is less than 80%.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome describes agreement of the melting temperature within 0.5 meV/atom, but meV/atom is an energy unit rather than a temperature unit. The falsification experiment more coherently applies this threshold to the free-energy difference.

The stated 2-3 meV/atom SRO stabilization is assigned to the solid phase, whereas the listed falsification measurements specify SRO parameters only in the liquid phase, so the experiment does not directly validate the claimed solid-phase contribution.
